blocks.body:
What is the last digit of $7^{2026}$? What is the remainder when $2^{100}$ is divided by $13$? You cannot compute these numbers in full by hand, and you do not need to: only remainders matter, and remainders can be added and multiplied on their own, throwing away everything else.

Gauss made this idea into a notation in 1801. Writing $a \equiv b \pmod n$ for "$a$ and $b$ leave the same remainder on division by $n$" lets you manipulate remainders almost exactly like equations. Nearly every olympiad number theory problem is phrased in this language, and this lesson sets it up carefully, including the one place where the analogy with equations breaks.

blocks.title: Congruence
blocks.body:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Integers $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$, written
$$a \equiv b \pmod n,$$
if $n \mid a - b$. The number $n$ is the modulus.

So $a \equiv b \pmod n$ means $a$ and $b$ differ by a multiple of $n$; for instance $17 \equiv 2 \pmod 5$ and $-3 \equiv 9 \pmod{12}$.

blocks.title: Same remainder, same class
blocks.body:
The definition is about differences, but it is the same as "same remainder". Write $a = nq + r$ and $b = nq' + r'$ with $0 \le r, r' < n$. Then $a - b = n(q - q') + (r - r')$, so $n \mid a - b$ exactly when $n \mid r - r'$. Since $|r - r'| < n$, that happens only when $r = r'$.

Congruence modulo $n$ behaves like equality in three ways: $a \equiv a$; if $a \equiv b$ then $b \equiv a$; and if $a \equiv b$ and $b \equiv c$ then $a \equiv c$ (add the two differences). So the integers split into $n$ classes, called residue classes, according to their remainder. Modulo $3$ the classes are
$$\{\dots, -3, 0, 3, 6, \dots\}, \quad \{\dots, -2, 1, 4, 7, \dots\}, \quad \{\dots, -1, 2, 5, 8, \dots\}.$$
Any choice of one number from each class, such as $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ or $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ for $n = 3$, is called a complete residue system. Choosing the representatives cleverly (often including negative ones) is a large part of the art.

blocks.title: Congruences can be added and multiplied
blocks.body:
If $a \equiv b \pmod n$ and $c \equiv d \pmod n$, then
$$a + c \equiv b + d \pmod n \quad \text{and} \quad ac \equiv bd \pmod n.$$
Consequently $a^k \equiv b^k \pmod n$ for every $k \ge 1$, and $P(a) \equiv P(b) \pmod n$ for every polynomial $P$ with integer coefficients.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Write $a - b = ns$ and $c - d = nt$. Then $(a + c) - (b + d) = n(s + t)$. For the product, add and subtract $bc$:
$$ac - bd = (a - b)c + b(c - d) = n(sc + bt).$$
Applying the product rule $k - 1$ times to $a \equiv b$ gives $a^k \equiv b^k$. A polynomial with integer coefficients is built from its variable and integers by additions and multiplications, so $P(a) \equiv P(b)$.

blocks.title: Arithmetic in Z/nZ
blocks.body:
The theorem says that the residue classes modulo $n$ can themselves be added and multiplied: to multiply two classes, multiply any representatives and take the class of the result; the answer does not depend on the choices. The resulting number system with $n$ elements is written $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. Algebraically it is a commutative ring, which means the familiar laws (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, $0$ and $1$) all hold.

In practice this means: reduce early and often. To find $7^{2026} \bmod 10$, notice $7^2 = 49 \equiv -1$, so $7^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}$. As $2026 = 4 \cdot 506 + 2$,
$$7^{2026} = (7^4)^{506} \cdot 7^2 \equiv 1 \cdot 49 \equiv 9 \pmod{10}.$$
The last digit is $9$.

Another classical application is digit tests. Since $10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9$, a number $\overline{d_k \dots d_1 d_0} = \sum d_i 10^i$ is congruent to $\sum d_i$ modulo $9$: a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by $9$ (and by $3$). Since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, the number is congruent modulo $11$ to the alternating sum $d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - \cdots$.

blocks.title: Cancellation: the one trap
blocks.body:
Addition, subtraction and multiplication work perfectly. Division does not. Modulo $6$,
$$2 \cdot 4 \equiv 2 \cdot 1 \pmod 6 \quad (\text{both are } \equiv 2), \qquad \text{but} \quad 4 \not\equiv 1 \pmod 6.$$
Worse, $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 6$ although neither factor is $\equiv 0$. Such zero divisors exist modulo every composite $n$.

The correct rule is: if $ac \equiv bc \pmod n$ and $\gcd(c, n) = 1$, then $a \equiv b \pmod n$.

Proof: we know $n \mid c(a - b)$, and we may assume $a \ne b$. By the Euclidean algorithm scaled by $|a - b|$ (see [[divisibility]]), $\gcd(n|a-b|,\ c|a-b|) = |a - b| \gcd(n, c) = |a - b|$. Now $n$ divides both $n|a-b|$ and $c|a-b|$, so it divides their gcd $|a - b|$.

Without coprimality you can still cancel, but you must shrink the modulus: if $ac \equiv bc \pmod n$ then $a \equiv b \pmod{n/\gcd(c,n)}$. In the example above, $2\cdot 4 \equiv 2 \cdot 1 \pmod 6$ gives $4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, which is true. The full theory of division, with inverses, is in [[mod-inverse]].

blocks.title: A large power
blocks.body: Find the remainder of $2^{100}$ on division by $13$.
blocks.solution:
Look for a small power of $2$ that is $\pm 1$ modulo $13$: $2^6 = 64 = 5 \cdot 13 - 1$, so $2^6 \equiv -1$ and $2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$. Since $100 = 12 \cdot 8 + 4$,
$$2^{100} = (2^{12})^8 \cdot 2^4 \equiv 1 \cdot 16 \equiv 3 \pmod{13}.$$
The remainder is $3$.

blocks.title: The test for 11
blocks.body: Without dividing, decide whether $918082$ is divisible by $11$.
blocks.solution:
Since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, we have $10^i \equiv (-1)^i$. Reading the digits from the units end, $2, 8, 0, 8, 1, 9$, the number is congruent to
$$2 - 8 + 0 - 8 + 1 - 9 = -22 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}.$$
So it is divisible by $11$; indeed $918082 = 11 \cdot 83462$.

blocks.title: An impossibility proof
blocks.body: Show that no integer of the form $8k + 7$ is a sum of three perfect squares.
blocks.solution:
Work modulo $8$. Every integer is congruent to one of $0, \pm1, \pm2, \pm3, 4$, and their squares are
$$0^2 = 0,\quad (\pm1)^2 = 1,\quad (\pm 2)^2 = 4,\quad (\pm 3)^2 = 9 \equiv 1,\quad 4^2 = 16 \equiv 0.$$
So every square is $\equiv 0, 1$ or $4 \pmod 8$. There are ten ways to add three values from $\{0, 1, 4\}$ (order does not matter):
$$0, 1, 2, 3 \ \ (\text{no } 4\text{s}), \qquad 4, 5, 6 \ \ (\text{one } 4), \qquad 8, 9 \ \ (\text{two } 4\text{s}), \qquad 12 \ \ (\text{three } 4\text{s}).$$
Modulo $8$ these are $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 0, 1, 4$. The residue $7$ never appears, so $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 8k + 7$ has no integer solutions.

This is the typical shape of an impossibility proof: find a modulus where the two sides cannot match. (Legendre showed that the numbers which are not sums of three squares are exactly those of the form $4^a(8k+7)$; see [[sums-of-squares]].)

blocks.title: Euler's factor of a Fermat number
blocks.body: Fermat conjectured that every number $2^{2^m} + 1$ is prime. Show that $641$ divides $2^{32} + 1$.
blocks.solution:
The number $641$ has two special forms: $641 = 5 \cdot 2^7 + 1$ and $641 = 5^4 + 2^4$. From the first,
$$5 \cdot 2^7 \equiv -1 \pmod{641}, \quad \text{so} \quad 5^4 \cdot 2^{28} \equiv (-1)^4 = 1 \pmod{641}.$$
From the second, $5^4 \equiv -2^4 \pmod{641}$. Substituting,
$$-2^4 \cdot 2^{28} \equiv 1, \quad \text{that is} \quad 2^{32} \equiv -1 \pmod{641}.$$
So $641 \mid 2^{32} + 1$, and Fermat's conjecture fails for $m = 5$. Euler found this factor in 1732. Notice that no large number was ever computed: the two special forms of $641$ did all the work.

blocks.body:
- Do not cancel a common factor unless it is coprime to the modulus: $2 \cdot 4 \equiv 2 \cdot 1 \pmod 6$ but $4 \not\equiv 1$.
- Exponents cannot be reduced modulo $n$. Although $5 \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, we have $2^5 = 32 \equiv 2$ while $2^0 = 1$. (Exponents can be reduced modulo something else; see [[fermat-euler]].)
- $x^2 \equiv y^2$ does not imply $x \equiv \pm y$ for composite moduli: $1^2 \equiv 3^2 \pmod 8$, yet $3 \not\equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8$.
- A congruence with a fraction such as $x \equiv \frac12 \pmod 7$ means nothing until you say which residue plays the role of $\frac12$ (here $4$, since $2 \cdot 4 \equiv 1$).
- Be careful with negative numbers: $-7 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, so its least non-negative residue is $2$.

Division modulo $n$ is the topic of [[mod-inverse]], and the reason $2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$ was no accident is [[fermat-euler]]. Passing from a prime modulus $p$ to $p^2, p^3, \dots$ is [[hensel]]. Digit tests generalise to [[digits-bases]], and the fact that $a - b \mid P(a) - P(b)$ for integer polynomials, which for $a \ne b$ is just $P(a) \equiv P(b) \pmod{|a-b|}$, is a basic tool in [[integer-polynomials]]. Modular obstructions like the one for $8k+7$ are the first thing to try on any [[diophantine]] equation; deciding which numbers are squares modulo $p$ is [[quadratic-residues]].

Further on, counting points on curves modulo $p$ is central to [[elliptic-curves]], and sums of $e^{2\pi i f(x)/n}$ over residues are [[exponential-sums]]. In computing, check digits work this way: the ISBN-10 check digit is chosen so that a weighted digit sum is divisible by $11$, and IBAN uses a check modulo $97$. Hash tables reduce keys modulo a table size.

1. Find the remainder of $3^{100}$ on division by $7$.
2. Show that $n^3 - n$ is divisible by $6$ for every integer $n$.
3. Show that the last digit of a perfect square is never $2, 3, 7$ or $8$.
4. Show that $x^2 - 3y^2 = 2$ has no integer solutions.
